summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage under its Penal Code, whose amended provisions took effect in 2015. Section 131 defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without a reason permitted under Islamic law, and section 411(2) names same-sex intercourse as an offence under section 411(f). Section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalises marriage between two persons of the same sex. Penalties run to one year for unlawful marriage under section 410(a)(8), up to eight years for the conduct covered by sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d) with a supplementary 100 lashes available under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under section 412. The 2014 code extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons.

Capital punishment is not available for these offences. The record states that homosexual acts cannot be punished with death under Maldivian law, that executions have been suspended since 1953, and that under sections 92(k) and 1205 death is reserved for egregious purposeful killing; plans to restart executions were later abandoned.

No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule or care restriction appears anywhere in this record. Every codified offence and penalty described concerns same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity, and none based on sexual orientation. The provisions are framed by sex, and the record contains no guidance on how a trans person's gender would be classified under them.

The only enforcement action documented in this record is the arrest of two men, aged 56 and 27, on Dhaandhoo island on 29 August 2015 for homosexual activity in their private home following a public complaint. No later instance is documented. A 2020 foreign government country report found no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons, while noting that societal stigma likely discouraged reporting.

Documented violence against LGBT people in the record consists of the 2013 neck stabbing of gay blogger Hilath Rasheed in Male. The United Nations Population Fund reported that people perceived as homosexual or transgender in the Maldives were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to protect LGBTQ individuals; the government noted those recommendations without accepting them. In 2014 New Zealand granted asylum to gay Maldivian Abraham Naim on the basis that he was at risk of serious harm from state agents, after a President's Office spokesman commented that people seeking asylum over sexual-orientation discrimination would face prosecution on return.

Official posture at the United Nations is restrictive. The Maldives rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations covering matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, including matters relating to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. It rejected the 2011 and September 2014 United Nations resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity, signed a 2008 document opposing decriminalisation, and noted but did not accept 2015 recommendations to decriminalise consenting adult same-sex relations. The Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Travel guidance in the record reports that LGBTQ tourists are generally welcome at most private tourist islands, resorts and hotels, which are usually isolated from civilian population centres and are described as not subject to Islamic law, with alcohol sales offered as evidence; guides advise caution about displays of affection outside tourist areas. A local advocacy group warned in 2015 that tourists could face threats similar to those faced by residents.

The record contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people as a distinct group. Every description of tolerance or hostility in it refers to LGBTQ people generally, to homosexuality, or to homophobia.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Rights Measurement Initiative's 2024 summary report on the Maldives, based on a second survey of human-rights experts, found that experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers, as the groups at risk of empowerment-rights violations. In the same survey political participation scored relatively well at 6.4 out of 10, while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

The Maldives' own Universal Periodic Review report of April 2015 records the government's accounting for the first cycle: of 126 recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons, reporting full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights compilation for the same cycle, dated March 2015, records the country's reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and CRC alongside concerns including the Sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage.

The record's tolerance and hostility descriptions are drawn from LGBTQ-wide material rather than from anything measured for transgender people alone, so comparisons between the Maldives and other jurisdictions in it rest on sexual-orientation findings.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Anti-LGBTQ discrimination is described as pervasive and homosexuality as a social taboo, and the local LGBTQ movement is characterised by a local advocacy group as operating mostly online because of the intensity of homophobia in the country.

A 2020 foreign government country report found that local citizens who expressed support for LGBTI rights on social media were targeted with online harassment as apostates or irreligious, and that societal stigma likely discouraged reporting of abuse. The same report found no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons.

Residents face prosecution under the Penal Code provisions: the two men arrested on Dhaandhoo on 29 August 2015 were local residents aged 56 and 27 taken from a private home. In 2014 a President's Office spokesman stated that people who left the country claiming asylum over sexual-orientation discrimination would face prosecution on return.

The United Nations Population Fund reported that residents perceived as homosexual or transgender were targets of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform; those recommendations were noted by the government but not accepted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on capital punishment. A 2015 advocacy report stated that death-penalty provisions were theoretically in reach for these offences, while the legal analysis in the record states that homosexual acts cannot be punished with death, that executions have been suspended since 1953, and that death is available only for egregious purposeful killing. This conflict is unresolved in the record.

No transgender-specific violence figure, count or rate appears in the record, and no denominator or general homicide rate is given, so no trans-specific magnitude of risk can be established from it.

The most recent documented enforcement incident in this record is the arrest of 29 August 2015; no later instance is documented. The absence of later documentation does not establish the present situation.

The record does not state how a trans person's gender would be classified under the sex-based provisions of sections 410 and 411, whether gender markers on passports or other documents are recognised, or how a visitor whose documents and presentation differ would be treated at entry. No document, marker, screening or facility rule for trans travellers is sourced.

The claim that private tourist islands and resorts are not subject to Islamic law comes from travel guidance and advocacy statements rather than from a legal instrument. No source in the record establishes that the Penal Code does not apply at resorts, and the point is unresolved.

The 2015 Universal Periodic Review accounting does not identify which individual recommendations were rejected on grounds relating to sexual orientation or gender identity beyond the general statement that 60 recommendations covering such matters were rejected as contradicting the Islamic faith and the Constitution.
